\paragraph{Attribution and comparison.}
The bibliographic notes distinguish established results and proof ingredients from the particular full-BFGS statements below. They record the primary-literature comparison through 11 September 2026, rather than certify publication priority. Such historical and comparative notes are separate from the mathematical assertions paired with Lean proofs. \paragraph{Attribution and comparison.}
These families include established special cases: Guo--Lewis proves Euclidean-norm convergence in arbitrary finite dimension \cite[Corollary 4.2]{GL18}. The broader applications retain their own hypotheses and proofs. The existence of a known special case does not identify the complete family theorem with that earlier result.
% END ATTRIBUTION i.known_special_cases

% BEGIN ATTRIBUTION d.negative_context
\paragraph{Attribution and comparison.}
The unit-first search below is Lewis--Overton's Algorithm 4.6 \cite{LO}. Earlier negative results include their convex subgradient/exact-search construction with null steps \cite{NEG_LO08}, smooth globally nonconvex examples \cite{NEG_M04,NEG_M07,NEG_M14,NEG_DAI02,NEG_DAI13}, Clarke-stationary limits with descent directions \cite{NEG_LZ15}, and scaled memoryless BFGS failure \cite{NEG_AO21}. Those settings differ from the convex, differentiable-query, full-update statement here. The recent planar counterexample of Diao uses a smooth nonconvex objective and an escaping exact-search trajectory \cite{NEG_DIAO26}. No exact match for the complete theorem was identified in the documented search; this is not a priority certification.
% END ATTRIBUTION d.negative_context

% BEGIN ATTRIBUTION d.construction_tools
\paragraph{Attribution and comparison.}
Prescribing an algebraic orbit and then constructing an objective that realizes its update equations has substantial precedents in Mascarenhas's divergence constructions \cite{NEG_M04,NEG_M07,NEG_M14}. The convex interpolation and all-query containment below are specific additional properties. Preconditioned residual maps and rigorous root enclosures are standard validated-numerics tools; compare Rump \cite[Section 13.2, Theorem 13.3]{NEG_RUMP10}. Here the required rational inequalities have their own Lean proofs, with no external numerical computation imported as a proof.
% END ATTRIBUTION d.construction_tools

% BEGIN ATTRIBUTION l.negative_scope
\paragraph{Attribution and comparison.}
The negative-results comparisons in Module D apply here with the stated stronger convexity and different branch regularity. This chapter uses the fixed line-search pair displayed below; D's wider parameter family is not imported. The first three branches of the local finite-branch construction fail to be twice differentiable at the accumulation point. The simpler global quadratic-plus-maximum example does not establish failure arbitrarily near its true minimizer. These distinctions are essential when comparing the theorem with smooth nonconvex counterexamples \cite{NEG_M07,NEG_M14,NEG_DIAO26}.
% END ATTRIBUTION l.negative_scope

% BEGIN ATTRIBUTION l.stable_manifold
\paragraph{Attribution and comparison.}
The stable-manifold principle and graph-transform method are classical; this chapter already uses Dyatlov's exposition \cite[Sections 3--4]{DY}. The report-specific work identifies the derivative of the actual BFGS return map, certifies its spectral bounds, and applies the principle to that map. Its exact formal orbit construction is recorded with the proof correspondence.
% END ATTRIBUTION l.stable_manifold
